BBC: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review. By Nick Triggle, health correspondent. JSON-LD datePublished = dateModified = 2026-10-08T23:01:30Z; on-page byline 'Published 9 October 2026, 00:01 BST'. Embargo drop, inside the window.
'There is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism, an official review in England has found.' A rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years means cases 'now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups'.
Review calls for tougher regulation of private firms offering assessments for the NHS, citing concerns about quality and consistency, and a ban on advertising.
Concluded economic uncertainty combined with social media was driving an increase in mental health problems among young people.
COMMISSIONING HISTORY: ordered 10 months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and 'written off'.
Experts said diagnoses too often became labels defining people by their 'difficulties rather than their strengths and potential', harming prospects at school, in work and in relationships.
HARD FIGURE: children diagnosed with autism and ADHD before the age of 17 are around four times more likely to end up not in education, employment or training between 16 and 24.
Likely to feed into government policy on NHS services, benefits and support for young people not in education, employment or training.
CASE STUDY: the Watson family. Ryan and his wife knew there was something different with son Atlas at around 12-18 months. It took three years to get an autism assessment. Atlas, now nearly seven, is non-verbal, still wears nappies and relies on others for all daily care. Ryan: 'You basically go on the list and wait however long until you get to the top.' On the fear of mainstream school: 'We were terrified. Anyone who has a child like Atlas will have the same panic that they'll start in a mainstream school where it's not safe.' And: 'It was like I had two jobs. I was going to work and then coming home and dealing with these things.' Atlas was diagnosed only months before starting school.
